source_text: Non omittam ipsius etiam conversationis haereticae descriptionem, quam futilis, quam terrena, quam humana sit, sine gravitate, sine auctoritate, sine disciplina, ut fidei suae congruens. In primis quis catechumenus, quis fidelis, incertum est; pariter adeunt, pariter audiunt, pariter orant; etiam ethnici si supervenerint, sanctum canibus, et porcis margaritas, licet non veras, jactabunt. Simplicitatem volunt esse prostrationem disciplinae, cujus penes nos curam lenocinium vocant. Pacem quoque passim cum omnibus miscent: nihil enim interest illis, licet diversa tractantibus, dum ad unius veritatis expugnationem conspirent. Omnes tument, omnes scientiam pollicentur. Ante sunt perfecti catechumeni, quam edocti. Ipsae mulieres haereticae, quam procaces! quae audeant docere, contendere, exorcismos agere, curationes repromittere, forsitan et tingere. Ordinationes eorum temerariae, leves, inconstantes: nunc neophytos conlocant, nunc saeculo obstrictos, nunc apostatas nostros, ut gloria eos obligent, quia veritate non possunt. Nusquam facilius proficitur, quam in castris rebellium, ubi ipsum esse illic, promereri est. Itaque alius hodie episcopus, cras alius; hodie diaconus, qui cras lector; hodie presbyter, qui cras laicus: nam et laicis sacerdotalia munera injungunt.
pass_a_gloss: I will not omit also a description of the heretical conversation, how futile, how earthly, how human it is, without gravity, without authority, without discipline, so that it is congruent to their faith. First of all, who is a catechumen, who is a believer, is uncertain; they approach equally, they hear equally, they pray equally; even if pagans arrive, they will throw holy things to dogs and pearls to pigs, even if they are not true ones. They want simplicity to be a destruction of discipline, whose care in our case they call leniency. They also mix peace everywhere with all people: for nothing is of concern to them, although they handle different things, as long as they conspire to the overthrow of one truth. All of them are puffed up, all of them promise knowledge. Catechumens are perfect before they are taught. The heretical women, how shameless they are! who dare to teach, to argue, to perform exorcisms, to promise cures, and perhaps even to baptize. Their ordinations are reckless, light, inconstant: now they place the newly baptized, now those bound to the world, now our apostates, so that they may obligate them with glory, because they cannot with truth. Nowhere is it easier to make progress than in the camps of the rebels, where to be there itself is a merit. And so, one person is a bishop today, another person is a bishop tomorrow; one person is a deacon today, who is a lector tomorrow; one person is a presbyter today, who is a layperson tomorrow: for they also impose priestly duties on laypeople.

pass_b_english: I will not skip a description of their heretical way of life either—how futile, how earthly, how merely human it is, lacking gravity, authority, and discipline, so that it matches their faith. For a start, no one can tell who is a catechumen and who is a believer; they all approach together, listen together, pray together. Even if pagans show up, they will throw what is holy to dogs and pearls to pigs—though the pearls are not genuine (Matt 7:6). They want simplicity to count as the demolition of discipline, yet in our ranks they call the care of that discipline mere leniency. They also mix peace indiscriminately with everyone; nothing matters to them, even when they handle different things, as long as they conspire to overthrow the one truth. All of them are puffed up, all of them promise knowledge. Catechumens count as perfect before they are taught. Their women—how shameless they are! They dare to teach, to argue, to perform exorcisms, to promise cures, and perhaps even to baptize. Their ordinations are reckless, flimsy, and inconstant: today they install a neophyte, tomorrow a man still bound to the world, the next day one of our own apostates, so that glory may bind them, since truth cannot. Nowhere is promotion easier than in the rebel camp, where simply being there counts as merit. So one man is bishop today, another tomorrow; today a deacon, tomorrow a lector; today a presbyter, tomorrow a layman—for they even impose priestly duties on laypeople.
